documents.abstract: This teaching case examines the role of machine learning, deep learning, and artificial intelligence algorithms in the development and operation of self-driving cars. Using examples such as Waymo and Tesla, it explores how autonomous vehicles collect, process, and respond to real-time data through sensor systems, computer vision, object detection, and neural networks. The teaching case compares the functions of machine learning and deep learning in autonomous driving, emphasizing their importance in decision-making, pedestrian detection, traffic navigation, and safety improvement. It also discusses the potential benefits of autonomous vehicles, including increased convenience, reduced traffic accidents, improved fuel efficiency, enhanced accessibility, and more efficient transportation systems. At the same time, the teaching case addresses major concerns involving public trust, legal liability, cybersecurity, data privacy, infrastructure readiness, job displacement, and performance limitations in unusual driving conditions. By examining current applications and future possibilities, the teaching case argues that self-driving cars represent both a major technological advancement and a complex social challenge. Continued progress will depend on reliable algorithms, strong data security, regulatory guidance, public confidence, and responsible implementation.

This exploratory study evaluates the factual accuracy and error/hallucination types of three commercial generative AI chatbots-ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity-when answering local tourism information questions about purposively selected attractions in Wonju, South Korea.Wonju was chosen as a local-city case because heterogeneous tourism assets coexist with facility and access information that has recently changed.Researchers developed eighteen standardized questions for six attractions, covering location/accessibility, operating conditions, and historical or unique attributes.Official materials issued by local government, public agencies, and facility operators were used to construct the reference answers.Fifty-four first responses were requested on July 26, 2026, using new sessions and a common prompt.The responses were segmented into independently verifiable factual claims and judged against the reference evidence.One Gemini response was lost due to user-interface collection artefact; because no response text remained, it was treated as missing data rather than as a chatbot error.Of 92 evaluable factual claims, 89 were accurate, yielding a sample accuracy rate of 96.7%.No hallucination was observed in this limited dataset.The substantive errors comprised one recency error related to recently changed location information and two contradictory claims involving the interpretation of historical dates.At the response level, no statistically significant service differences among the 17 complete matched items.These findings are restricted to the sampled attractions, questions, services, and collection date.The study demonstrates that domain-specific evaluations of generative AI tourism information should distinguish factual accuracy, timeliness, source-context interpretation, and collection integrity, while avoiding broad generalization from a small exploratory sample.

Manufacturing safety is being digitalized through wearable sensors, connected-worker platforms, and artificial intelligence (AI), but the evidence does not yet justify treating a conceptual architecture as a validated predictive safety system.This study therefore proposes a conceptual design framework for integrating smart personal protective equipment (PPE) monitoring with future predictive analytics in smart manufacturing.We conducted a structured integrative synthesis of peerreviewed literature published from 2018 through September 2026 in Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and ScienceDirect, supplemented by targeted searches of occupational safety agencies, standards bodies, and primary manufacturer documentation.Search concepts combined smart PPE or workplace wearables with occupational safety, manufacturing, ergonomics, human-robot collaboration, IoT, anomaly detection, and machine learning.Sources were assembled by theoretical sampling from anchor reviews and their citation networks, and selection stopped at conceptual saturation of the framework's design space rather than at exhaustive coverage of the field.We coded eligible sources by industrial sector, hazard, sensing modality, connectivity, analytical method, validation maturity, and governance coverage against a published codebook.We organized recurrent capture-transmit-analyzeact functions into four technical layers.We linked them to a cross-cutting governance and assurance plane covering accountability, worker participation, purpose limitation, data access and retention, human decision authority, and algorithmic oversight.The resulting conceptual outputs distinguish calibrated rule-based alerts, statistical anomaly detection, supervised hazard classification, and prognostic modeling; specify candidate inputs, ground-truth labels, and validation metrics; and define controls for sensor drift, missing data, latency, false alarms, model drift, uncertainty, and alert fatigue.Numeric operational thresholds are intentionally excluded because no sensor system, dataset, simulation, or field trial was used.The contribution is therefore a traceable design framework and staged research agenda, not evidence of predictive performance or safety improvement.Future work must calibrate sensors, prospectively validate models across worker subgroups, evaluate human factors and privacy, and demonstrate that the system remains advisory relative to independently engineered safety controls.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study compared physical fitness, physical activity, and motivational climate among adolescent girls in Iran and Hungary within the frameworks of self-determination theory and achievement goal theory. A cross-sectional study was performed among 539 girl students aged 13–15 years (mean age = 13.93; SD = 0.82 years). Data were analysed using factorial ANOVA, independent t-tests, confirmatory factor analysis, and structural equation modelling. Hungarian students demonstrated higher performance in most physical fitness tests and had higher body mass index values (p = 0.002). Physical activity levels differed only at age 14 (p = 0.019, r = −0.18), with no significant differences at other ages. Iranian students reported higher perceptions of motivational climate dimensions. The measurement model showed good fit (χ2(143) = 1.81; CFI = 0.99; TLI = 0.99; SRMR = 0.03; RMSEA = 0.039), and structural equation modelling indicated that only task-involving climate was positively associated with physical activity (β = 0.325, p = 0.003), while other motivational dimensions were not significant. The findings demonstrated that although physical fitness and motivational climate dimensions differed across both countries, physical activity levels remained relatively similar among groups. This implies that intrinsic motivational climate may be related to physical activity participation. However, differences in physical activity levels in each country could be attributed to other variables such as education, culture, socioeconomic status, environment, among others. Task-involving climate emerged as the only dimension of motivational climate associated significantly with physical activity, suggesting a potential association between task-involving climate and active lifestyles among adolescent girls.

Examining energy-related issues and comfort conditions in residential buildings is essential for achieving sustainable development. Accordingly, this study aims to optimize building envelope design parameters—including air-tightness values derived from empirical measurements—to strike a balance between energy consumption, thermal comfort, and visual comfort. A multi-stage, systematic methodology is proposed, featuring a hybrid artificial intelligence-based framework for prediction and optimization, grounded in building performance simulations. A BlowerDoor test was conducted on the residential building under study, and the results were integrated into a building performance model. Data generated through these simulations were used to compare the performance of various machine learning meta-models, including Artificial Neural Networks, Support Vector Regression (SVR), and XGBoost. The SVR model, which demonstrated the lowest error rate and highest reliability across most objectives, was selected as the meta-model for the optimization phase. This model served as the objective function for a multi-objective optimization process carried out using the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II). The results of this surrogate-model-based optimization indicate a 21.69% reduction in energy consumption, alongside improvements of 17.2% in visual comfort and 20% in thermal comfort compared to the baseline state. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that air-tightness influences daylighting performance through its interaction with other parameters, such as the Window-to-Wall Ratio (WWR) and building orientation. Finally, the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) method was employed to determine the relative importance of the design parameters following the multi-objective optimization. The analysis results indicate that the order of influence of various parameters differs depending on the specific objective. While the window-to-wall ratio (WWR) and orientation are the primary factors for enhancing visual comfort, factors such as orientation, infiltration, and the thermal transmittance of building components are the most significant for improving energy efficiency and thermal comfort. Consequently, the integration of data-driven approaches—based on surrogate models—into building performance assessment can contribute significantly to the sustainability of residential buildings and offer a new research framework for future studies.

Abstract The number of artificial intelligence (AI) use cases relevant to health care has continued to increase substantially because technology has evolved. For orthopaedic surgeons and musculoskeletal providers, the onus has expanded beyond learning about these tools conceptually and shifted toward understanding how to use them in everyday clinical workflows. There is a perceived opportunity cost from ignoring these use cases and, similarly, an operational cost from excessively implementing AI tools without thoughtful consideration of how they may impact patient care. This infographic shows how orthopaedic surgeons may leverage various AI solutions to create a digital ecosystem that portends efficiency and value. Before a patient formally establishes care with a physician, AI solutions leveraging agentic frameworks may assist with scheduling appointments based on screening criteria, informing patients of outstanding laboratory or imaging requests, and curating physicians’ schedules. During appointments, physicians can leverage ambient scribes, which listen to patient‐physician encounters and automatically synthesize clinical notes, to make visits more efficient. Furthermore, more recent iterations of scribes automatically codify diagnoses and treatments using International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision and Current Procedural Terminology and prepopulate orders. The Hospital for Special Surgery, Cleveland Clinic, and Kaiser Permanente, among many others, have used these pipelines to reduce administrative burden and allow more time for direct patient interactions. Multimodal models trained on vast amounts of imaging data may allow for intelligent diagnosis of musculoskeletal pathologies; however, several advanced solutions allow physicians to create “digital twins” and model patient‐specific pathology to guide surgical techniques and predict optimal placement of grafts, implants, and/or tunnels. Postoperatively, physicians can leverage practice‐specific guidelines to create asynchronous chat agents to increase adherence to rehabilitation guidelines. Wearable devices allow real‐time transmission of motion data to help physicians understand recovery trajectory and progress against milestones. Important ethical questions remain. Patient privacy is paramount, requiring enterprise agreements with AI vendors to ensure data remains Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act‐compliant. Furthermore, systems need to implement governing boards, regular audits, and safety guardrails to ensure data safety and appropriate model performance. Significant literacy gaps remain among patients in underserved communities, so physicians must consider equitable AI implementation. As models progress in capability and speed and become less costly, physicians have exciting avenues to optimize clinical workflows and free more time for empathetic, patient‐guided care.

documents.abstract: Purpose: To evaluate the agreement of a digital twin–inspired patient-specific eye–lens simulation framework and reference-standard subjective refraction for pediatric postcycloplegic spectacle prescription. Methods: In this prospective randomized testing sequence agreement study, 183 right eyes from 183 children (mean age, 9.9 ± 2.0 years) underwent traditional autorefraction, artificial intelligence (AI) wavefront refraction, and masked subjective refraction. The framework used microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) Shack–Hartmann wavefront data, image quality gating, virtual trial-lens simulation, and perturbation-aware optimization to generate an AI-based prescription estimate. Agreement was assessed for spherical equivalent (SE), Jackson cross-cylinder component at axis 0° (J0), and Jackson cross-cylinder component at axis 45° (J45). Results: Traditional autorefraction differed significantly from subjective refraction in SE, J0, and J45: 0.21 ± 0.52 diopters (D) for SE (P < 0.001), −0.04 ± 0.21 D for J0 (P = 0.006), and 0.02 ± 0.13 D for J45 (P = 0.037). AI wavefront refraction showed smaller mean differences without statistically significant differences: 0.04 ± 0.35 D for SE (P = 0.153), −0.01 ± 0.19 D for J0 (P = 0.681), and 0.00 ± 0.15 D for J45 (P = 0.725). For SE, AI wavefront refraction showed narrower 95% limits of agreement than traditional autorefraction (−0.67 to 0.74 D vs. −0.81 to 1.22 D) and higher proportions within ≤0.25 D and ≤0.50 D (66.1% vs. 54.6%; 91.3% vs. 86.9%). Conclusions: The digital twin–inspired patient-specific eye–lens simulation framework generated pediatric postcycloplegic prescription estimates that agreed more closely with subjective refraction than traditional autorefraction, particularly for SE. These findings support its feasibility as an upstream decision support component, although real-world spectacle wear feedback and longitudinal model updating require further study. Translational Relevance: This study provides prospective clinical validation for an upstream component of a future human-in-the-loop ophthalmic digital twin for spectacle prescription by translating patient-specific wavefront data into virtual trial-lens simulation and AI-assisted refraction decision support.

Abstract Marine structures such as ships and offshore platforms often suffer structural deformation during service due to factors including collision and corrosion. After deformation occurs, the rapid evaluation of the hydrodynamic performance of structures is a prerequisite for ensuring safety and formulating maintenance strategies. To this end, this paper establishes a rapid evaluation framework for the hydrodynamic performance of deformed marine structures, which integrates image acquisition, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based Three-Dimensional (3D) reconstruction, numerical simulation, and emergency decision-making. The specific procedure of the framework consists of four steps: First, a multi-view image acquisition scheme for structures considering deformed regions is designed to collect two-dimensional images and complete preprocessing. Second, the 3D model of the structure is reconstructed based on the HunYuan3D model, followed by preprocessing operations such as hole filling and topological repair. Third, the processed model is imported into hydrodynamic software to complete the numerical simulation and performance evaluation of the structure. Finally, a follow-up disposal plan is formulated and decision-making suggestions are provided based on the evaluation results.The framework is validated on a deformed ship: the errors of the governing geometric parameters of the reconstructed model are within 3%, and the simulated deterioration of the stability reserve and motion responses is consistent with the mechanisms reported for damaged hulls. Positioning the framework as a rapid preliminary screening and decision-support tool for emergency scenarios, the results demonstrate an efficient evaluation of the hydrodynamic performance of deformed structures with a balance among low cost, high efficiency, and verifiable reliability, providing data support for the emergency decision-making of deformed ships and offshore platforms.

Firefighting imposes concurrent physical and cognitive demands, whereas few laboratory paradigms replicate these dual-task challenges. This study developed an experimental protocol for inducing psychophysiological strain in firefighters. Twenty male firefighters (25.8 ± 3.4 years) completed a structured protocol consisting of a speech task (ST), a combined task involving load carriage with serial subtraction, and a physical task simulating hose-running. Salivary cortisol, α-amylase (sAA), dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), heart rate variability (HRV), and electrodermal activity were measured. Results showed marked activation of the endocrine responses, with significant increases in cortisol (122%), sAA (108%), and DHEA (138%) (all p < 0.001). Additionally, heart rate increased significantly during the ST (p = 0.007). HRV indices demonstrated pronounced autonomic modulation across stress stages. These findings support the protocol as a standardised tool for simulating occupational stress in firefighters, with potential applications in strain monitoring, protective equipment design, and wearable system development.
topics: Heart Rate Variability and Autonomic Control

documents.abstract: This article examines the pedagogical and methodological aspects of improving teaching effectiveness through digital learning platforms integrated with artificial intelligence (AI). It analyzes the didactic potential of AI technologies in digital learning environments, the organization of learning processes adapted to students’ individual needs, the development of independent learning activities, and mechanisms for assessing knowledge and learning outcomes. The article also explores the application of AI tools in adaptive, blended, distance, synchronous, and asynchronous learning. A methodological approach aimed at improving teaching effectiveness through the integration of AI into digital learning platforms is proposed. The main components of this approach, criteria for assessing effectiveness, existing challenges, and possible solutions are discussed. The proposed methodology emphasizes the integration of digital platforms, AI tools, pedagogical strategies, and assessment mechanisms within a unified educational framework.

Purpose: This study aims to develop and evaluate an adaptive ergonomic framework for reducing Musculoskeletal Disorder (MSD) risks among pre-elderly workers in Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs). Methodology: This study adopted a sequential quantitative design consisting of two consecutive phases. The first phase involved a cross-sectional ergonomic assessment of 50 pre-elderly MSMEs workers using the Nordic Body Map (NBM), Rapid Entire Body Assessment (REBA), Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA), and Quick Exposure Checklist (QEC). Based on the integrated assessment results, an adaptive ergonomic framework incorporating administrative controls, engineering controls, ergonomic personal protective equipment (PPE), and anthropometry-based workstation redesign was developed. The second phase evaluated the framework through a 14-day before–after intervention study in five selected MSMEs. Results: Most workers were exposed to moderate-to-very high ergonomic risks, with musculoskeletal complaints predominantly affecting the lower back, back, wrists, neck, and lower extremities. Following implementation, QEC exposure scores decreased across the five MSMEs from 68.7–84.5% before intervention to 46.3–63.2% after intervention, accompanied by reductions in REBA/RULA risk classifications and lower NBM complaint levels. Conclusion: The proposed framework effectively reduced ergonomic risks and musculoskeletal complaints among pre-elderly MSMEs workers through practical and low-cost interventions. Originality: This study contributes a comprehensive and context-specific adaptive ergonomic framework that integrates risk assessment, workstation redesign, administrative controls, and ergonomic PPE recommendations tailored to the characteristics of pre-elderly workers in resource-constrained MSMEs.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Local service businesses can steady their lead flow by adding a third, owner-controlled channel: researched, personalized outreach to a defined list of property owners and decision-makers. Paid ads and referrals are the usual two. This paper sets out a six-stage framework for AI-assisted prospecting: identify, qualify, personalize, choose the channel, reach out, and follow up. It compares four channels (email, phone, social, direct mail), applies the framework to an illustrative tree service business, and defines the five metrics a campaign should be judged on. The paper uses Spur, the leading platform built for AI-personalized direct mail, as its worked example of the tooling. Spur (usespur.com) also connects to AI assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT. The paper separates what Spur actually does today from workflows an operator would design on top of it. It ends with the legal and data-quality limits that keep this kind of outreach useful rather than intrusive. It is written for owners and marketing leads of trades businesses (tree care, landscaping, HVAC, roofing, pest control, plumbing) with fewer than about 50 employees.

Scope and status This document proposes a practical review protocol for teams that exchange small animated vector graphics for use in web interfaces. It is a methods note, not a completed study, a dataset, a benchmark or a claim about measured accessibility. The protocol is intended to help an author state what a graphic is meant to communicate, preserve an editable source and describe what has and has not been checked. It can be adapted for an icon, logo, decorative indicator or other small graphic. The examples are hypothetical and do not report actual participants or user outcomes. The document is associated with the SVG Animation project. Artificial intelligence assisted with drafting and editing the text. The project provides a browser-based workflow for SVG source editing, motion presets, optional AI assistance, and SVG, GIF or MP4 export. Its public homepage is animated svg. Consult that site for current features, limits and pricing. Mention of the project is not an independent evaluation or institutional endorsement, and the protocol does not require the project to be used. The author must hold the rights needed to share any artwork, source file or screenshot included in a later application of this protocol. Define the communication task A review begins by identifying the question the movement is expected to answer. For an interface indicator, the question might be whether a state has changed. For a decorative emblem, the goal might be to add visual rhythm without conveying a system status. These are different tasks. A decorative loop should not silently become the only sign of a significant error, and a status cue should not depend entirely on an aesthetic interpretation. Write a short purpose statement and identify whether the graphic is essential to the message or can be removed without losing information. Record the trigger separately from the artwork. An SVG file can contain animation instructions, but the surrounding application determines when the graphic is shown and what events it represents. The review should identify who is responsible for connecting the cue to application state. If the state is only simulated in a design preview, call it a simulation. Do not describe a real-time integration as complete until it has actually been implemented and checked in the receiving environment. Establish a baseline Before comparing motion variants, prepare a static baseline using the same visual elements. Check whether the graphic is recognizable at the intended size, whether it obscures neighboring text, and whether the contrast remains adequate over representative backgrounds. The selection of backgrounds should reflect the planned use rather than a promise to cover every screen. Note which sizes and backgrounds were inspected and which are still open questions. The static baseline also gives reviewers a meaningful alternative. If a moving effect makes a status less clear than the still image, the team can simplify it or retain the static treatment. A baseline is not automatically an accessible fallback: it must communicate the relevant information, and the application must actually provide it in the circumstances for which it is intended. The review record should distinguish a proposed alternative from one already implemented. Describe the candidate motion For each candidate, list the visible starting state, the transition, the resting state and the expected behavior at the loop boundary. The record need not contain every keyframe. It should be specific enough that another person can understand what is being compared. If two alternatives differ only in duration, keep the artwork and placement stable while reviewing them. If several properties change together, identify that limitation rather than attributing a difference in perception to a single parameter. Record whether motion is triggered once, repeated, or controlled by external state. Consider what happens when a scene changes midway through a transition or when a component is removed and reinserted. These questions cannot be settled merely by replaying an isolated animation. They belong to the integration plan and should be checked in the actual application when an implementation is available. A note that an interruption test remains unperformed is more useful than an unsupported statement that the animation is robust. Consider reduced motion and readable alternatives A responsible handoff describes what should happen when movement is reduced or unavailable. Depending on the purpose, a static icon, direct text label or shorter transition may be a suitable alternative. When a graphic communicates an important state, confirm that reducing the motion does not remove the only way to perceive that state. For a decorative element, disabling it entirely may be a reasonable choice. The specific decision should be documented alongside the reason. Reviewers should not infer conformance with a standard from the presence of a fallback alone. Record the relevant settings, browsers, devices and assistive technologies only if they were actually tested. If a review relies on visual inspection, describe it as visual inspection. A later formal accessibility assessment may use this protocol as a starting record, but it requires its own criteria, evidence and appropriate expertise. Track source, previews and exports Keep the editable source distinct from review copies. A small animated GIF can be convenient in a message, but it may omit information needed for later changes. An MP4 may be useful for a presentation, while an SVG may be more appropriate for a web implementation. These formats differ in editing, transparency, scaling and playback behavior. The protocol does not assume that one export format is always superior. Assign a clear version label to each file and identify which source produced each preview. Record dimensions, export settings and the destination application when those details are available. Before sharing, open the actual exported file in the environment for which it is intended. A button that offers an export is not evidence that every receiver can use the resulting file, and an attractive preview is not proof that an application will respect a reduced-motion setting. Preserve rights and private information Use material that the author is permitted to edit and distribute. A demonstration can use invented shapes and neutral labels instead of private client artwork or a real user record. If a screenshot includes personal information, determine whether it is necessary for the review and remove or protect it before sharing. Document any external font, image or code dependency whose rights or availability could affect a handoff. This text may be shared under the license stated in its repository record. That license applies to the original text in this document only. It does not grant rights to a third-party product, its source code, logos, exported artwork or separately linked materials. The presence of a website link is a reference to the project and should not be interpreted as permission to reuse all content found there. Use a concise review card The following fields provide a minimal starting point: graphic name and version; intended purpose; trigger and expected resting state; destination and approximate display size; static or reduced-motion alternative; source filename; preview and export filenames; tests actually performed; known limitations; and a contact or owner for the next decision. An empty field can be marked unknown or not yet tested. Do not fill it with an invented result simply to make the card appear complete. Comments should describe observations in context. For example, a reviewer might say that a label was difficult to read at a particular window width while the overlay crossed it. That observation is more useful than a vague instruction to improve the design. If the issue is hypothetical, label it as hypothetical. If the person testing used only a preview image, do not represent the observation as a production-browser test. Decision and revision At the end of a review, record whether the candidate was accepted for a defined context, needs revision, or remains undecided. An approval for one setting does not automatically extend to every device or publication. Keep the previous editable version when feasible, describe what changed, and revisit the decision if the surrounding layout, playback environment or content changes substantially. This protocol is deliberately prospective. It offers a structure for a future review rather than a claim that one has occurred. Its value is in making assumptions visible: the task of the animation, the conditions of inspection, the location of the source and the boundaries of the evidence. A team can shorten or expand the card to fit its work, provided it continues to separate what was proposed, what was actually observed and what still requires testing.

The aim of this study is to examine individuals’ views and expectations regarding the hybrid human–artificial intelligence relationship that could be established in the workplace within the Turkish context. The study was conducted using a qualitative research design. A semi-structured questionnaire was used. Data were analysed using the Straussian grounded theory approach through open, axial and selective coding. A total of 92 participants were recruited using a purposive sampling method. Themes and codes were developed based on participants’ statements using open, axial and selective coding methods, supported by the MAXQDA v.2020 analysis software. The findings of the study revealed that, rather than a hybrid model, there is a need to distinguish between concepts based on human and robotic systems, and highlighted the necessity for human characteristics and technology management under human control to be present in the workplace. The participants considered the preservation of human qualities such as empathy, conscience, ethical sensitivity and cultural awareness to be important; whilst expressing views on the use of artificial intelligence and robotic systems in areas such as analytical thinking, systematic work, speed and reducing the workload. The research was evaluated within the framework of socio-technical systems theory and provided insights into how social and technical structures can be integrated within hybrid working systems.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: This study aimed to explore nursing students' experiences of understanding course topics and peer relationships through participation in Role-Playing activities.It also examined the significance of these Role-Playing experiences in shaping students' academic self-efficacy and professional nursing competencies.The researchers collected data through reflective journals and in-depth interviews with 12 nursing students who participated in an Adult Health Nursing course.The collected data were analyzed using a phenomenological research method.The study results revealed the following: First, participants experienced an "enhanced understanding" of the diseases covered in the course topics while preparing for and performing the role-play.Second, through the interaction and collaboration required for preparation, they developed a sense of "closeness and respect" toward peers they had not previously known well.Third, while constructing case studies and writing scenarios based on the diseases in the curriculum, they experienced "empathy and a shift in perception" regarding the professional attitudes required of future nurses.Fourth, through the role-playing activities, they gained a fresh perspective on learning, interpersonal relationships, and the nursing profession, resulting in a satisfying experience of "discovering meaning."Based on these findings, the following suggestions are made: First, major courses should use diverse participatory teaching and learning methods, such as Role-Playing, rather than relying solely on traditional lectures.In particular, given the current educational landscape that incorporates various learning materials and technologies (including generative AI), it is essential to create an environment that encourages active student participation and moves away from passive knowledge transmission.Second, to conduct role-playing activities effectively, integrate pre-and postlearning sessions that build understanding of the relevant medical conditions.This integrated learning helps alleviate the difficulties learners face when developing case studies and scenarios suited to the role-play themes, transforming challenges into positive insights gained through peer interaction and enhancing academic selfefficacy by allowing repeated review and deeper engagement with the material.Furthermore, systematic learning through role play can serve as an effective teaching-learning strategy to improve nursing students' clinical competence, thereby contributing to the cultivation of the essential skills required of future professional nurses.
topics: Innovative Teaching Methodologies in Social Sciences

documents.abstract: Community Question Answering (CQA) platforms function as continuously evolving repositories of user-generated knowledge, where questions are often informal, intents may be multiple, evidence is distributed across sources, and knowledge changes over time. These characteristics limit the applicability of conventional single-label and single-document approaches to complex information needs. This review traces the evolution of CQA from retrieval and ranking through neural semantic matching and pretrained Transformer models to retrieval-augmented generation and large language models, with particular emphasis on multi-label question understanding and multi-document evidence integration. Existing studies are compared from the perspectives of semantic representation, intent modeling, evidence retrieval and fusion, knowledge grounding, and answer reliability. The literature shows that substantial progress has been made in individual capabilities, but a unified mechanism that coordinates multi-label intent interpretation, dynamic retrieval, evidence verification, and grounded generation remains insufficiently developed. Future research should therefore move toward closed-loop architectures and evaluation frameworks that jointly measure label identification, evidence coverage, source attribution, and final answer quality in realistic community settings.

A basic premise of standard machine learning is that the training set and the test set come from the same distribution, but this premise is often broken in practice. Text classification is one of the most fundamental tasks in natural language processing (NLP). The poor robustness of its models to out-of-distribution (OOD) samples has become an important research topic. This study reviews the latest research on OOD generalization in text classification. First, it defines OOD generalization, which can be viewed from the data perspective as systematic data variance and from the model perspective as distorted features. Second, it introduces domain generalization methods, anti-shortcut feature learning, solutions for class distribution shift, and the main methods for OOD generalization of large language models. Then, it presents evaluation benchmarks and datasets used for three types of evaluation: distribution shift, compositional generalization, and class distribution shift. Finally, it identifies the limitations of existing studies and proposes future research directions.

In source code vulnerability detection, large language models (LLMs) are no longer used only as substitutes for traditional fixed classifiers. With prompt design, parameter fine-tuning, and program-context information, they can judge whether code contains vulnerabilities and can also provide suspicious locations and explanatory evidence. This paper takes lightweight code Transformers and large-scale language models as two main lines of discussion. It reviews methods for input construction, task adaptation, the use of program-analysis information, and multi-model collaboration, and compares them in terms of datasets, evaluation metrics, and deployment conditions. Existing studies show that code pretraining, prompt engineering, supervised fine-tuning, and structural-information enhancement can improve detection or explanation results on specific benchmarks. However, such improvements are easily affected by duplicate samples, label noise, random splits, temporal leakage, and changes in model versions, which may lead to overestimated performance. Therefore, model evaluation should not rely on a single metric alone. It should also report the data source, detection granularity, temporal or project-level isolation, false-positive cost, and whether generated explanations can be verified by program evidence. On this basis, this paper further discusses an application approach centered on data governance, strict data splitting, uncertainty calibration, and SAST-LLM-human collaboration. The discussion is limited to source-code-level vulnerability detection, localization, and classification, and does not cover network intrusion detection, malware analysis, smart-contract-specific detection, vulnerability generation, or automatic repair.

Agentic AI describes systems based on foundation models that extend generative AI from passive response generation toward executing tasks to achieve specific goals through planning, tool use, memory, reflection, multi-agent coordination, and environmental interaction. This scoping review maps recent peer-reviewed research on Agentic AI to clarify its conceptual foundations, application domains, technical patterns, risks, and future directions. Following PRISMA-ScR guidance, searches were conducted in IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and ScienceDirect for studies published between 2017 and June 2026. A total of 3549 records were identified, 3308 records were screened after duplicate removal, and 163 included studies were synthesized. The findings show that Agentic AI is commonly operationalized through LLM or foundation model reasoning combined with multi-step task decomposition, tool or API use, RAG, memory, reflection, and multi-agent coordination. Major application areas include cybersecurity, privacy and compliance; networks and telecommunications; robotics and embodied AI; software engineering, DevOps and EDA; and knowledge, data, and multimodal analytics. A post hoc ACM Digital Library and Scopus conference-coverage sensitivity analysis showed that application-domain proportions were sensitive to database and document-type coverage, whereas the main recurring architectural signals remained qualitatively stable. Recurring technical patterns include governance middleware, collaborative and hierarchical multi-agent architectures, memory-enabled agency, executable reasoning, and closed-loop validation. Reported risks include hallucination propagation, unsafe tool use, memory poisoning, privacy leakage, prompt injection, coordination failure, cost, latency, scalability, and human-oversight challenges. Future research should prioritize real-world validation, standardized benchmarks, runtime governance, secure memory management, human oversight, and cross-domain generalization.

After the adoption of Generative AI (GenAI) tools in 2022, research on AI literacy in education is a growing field. Less attention has been given to how teacher educators engage with these technologies in practice. Drawing on a digital agency perspective on professional knowledge and AI literacy, this study reports findings from an exploratory self-study. We investigate how we, as three teacher educators, engaged with GenAI in the design and delivery of Small Private Online Courses (SPOCs). Our study identifies four situated epistemic practices emerging through negotiated engagement with GenAI, which, to varying degrees, challenge our professional judgement and identity as teacher educators, taking practice-stabilizing and practice-transgressive forms. Each of these aligns with AI literacy dimensions described in existing frameworks. The findings show how AI literacy is enacted in situated contexts, where teacher educators’ professional judgement is central rather than a stable digital competence. The study contributes to research on teacher educators’ AI literacy and professional knowledge.

ABSTRACT Existing research has primarily conceptualized generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) as an instrumental technology that enhances employees' task capabilities and work outcomes, leaving unclear whether and how interactions with GenAI may shape employees' sense of self. This question is important because GenAI may influence not only what employees accomplish but also how they perceive their own knowledge and capabilities, which are critical for adapting to changing work demands. Drawing on self‐expansion theory, we propose that GenAI usage enhances employees' adaptive performance by fostering self‐expansion and that perceived GenAI–self similarity strengthens this process. We tested the proposed model using a three‐wave time‐lagged survey of 220 full‐time employees in China. Results showed that GenAI usage fostered self‐expansion, which subsequently enhanced adaptive performance, and this indirect effect was stronger among employees with higher GenAI–self similarity. By highlighting self‐expansion as a process through which GenAI‐enabled knowledge, perspectives, and capabilities can become incorporated into employees' self‐concepts, this study provides a self‐expansion perspective on human–GenAI augmentation and identifies perceived GenAI–self similarity as an important boundary condition of this process.

Since September 2026 one AI agent, Hermes, has done most of the drafting behind my job as Director of Research Computing at UC Riverside. I call it my seneschal, the old word for a steward who ran a household in the owner's name and answered to the owner. It drafts email, ticket notes and ledger entries. I approve the exact text before anything leaves. Two of my tools enforce that approval in code. On the path I use most, it is a written rule the agent follows. On 28 October 2026 the work ledger picked up 15 entries. Eleven record an email that went out after I approved the text. In nine of those the agent says it then found the message in my Sent folder, which is the agent checking itself. None of the 11 mentions the code-enforced composer. I trust the setup because of the approval step and the log, and the log is less complete than I would like. Field Notes technical report. Web edition: https://charles-forsyth.github.io/papers/2026-10-29-a-seneschal-for-the-research-computing-desk.html. This record holds the PDF (ACM sigconf, PDF/A-2b) and the LaTeX source.

documents.abstract: This paper presents a study on the implementation of Brazil’s General Data Protection Law within the public sector, with a specific focus on the São Paulo State Court of Justice. Through a survey-based research the paper discusses how public agents interpret, internalize, and operationalize the data protection legislation in their institutional routines. From a socio-institutional perspective, the study analyzes how legal compliance is shaped by organizational culture, hierarchical structures, cognitive schemas, and technological infrastructure. This perspective engages with the sociological framework of Pierre Bourdieu to conceptualize the State as a structured field in which agents’ positions, trajectories, and resources shape patterns of normative adherence. The results reveal heterogeneous patterns of adherence to data protection norms, conditioned by role-specific perspectives, institutional maturity, and sociotechnical factors. The paper demonstrates the relevance of the survey not merely as a diagnostic instrument but also as a reflexive mechanism capable of mapping the symbolic and behavioral landscape of legal implementation.

Artificial intelligence and spatial data technologies have expanded information-processing capabilities in public space design, but greater access to information does not necessarily improve design judgment.This study proposes a structural model linking spatial environmental cognition, behavior and needs identification, sociocultural understanding, multi-source information integration, design problem construction, human-AI collaborative judgment, and use feedback and dynamic optimization in rural public space design.A cross-sectional survey using purposive recruitment was conducted among professionals engaged in rural public space design and related development activities across eastern, central, western, and northeastern China.Of 500 questionnaires distributed, 468 valid responses were obtained.Confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling, and 5,000 bootstrap resamples were used to test the proposed relationships.The results showed that contextual cognition was significantly associated with multi-source information integration, which was further associated with design problem construction and human-AI collaborative judgment.Human-AI collaborative judgment was positively associated with use feedback and dynamic optimization.Significant indirect associations were also identified through multi-source information integration and design problem construction.These findings support a structural pathway from contextual cognition to information integration, task specification, collaborative judgment, and feedback updating in human-AI collaborative rural public space design.

documents.abstract: Introduction Women constitute a growing share of the hospitality workforce. Differences in gender consciousness between younger and older female hotel employees remain under-explored, particularly outside Western contexts, as do the factors that account for them. Methods This study examined such differences among 302 female hotel employees in China, drawing on an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design in which a structured survey of two age groups (151 aged 18 to 44 and 151 aged 45 and above) was followed by semi-structured interviews of ten employees (five from each age group). Grounded in social role theory and generational cohort theory, the survey examined two related gender-relevant constructs, feminine communal orientation and gender equality awareness, while interview data were used to explore participants’ interpretations of the observed differences. Results Younger employees showed significantly higher feminine communal orientation and more egalitarian gender attitudes than middle-aged and older employees in the primary group comparisons. After adjustment for educational attainment, hotel-industry tenure, and job level, the age-group difference in feminine communal orientation was attenuated and no longer statistically significant, whereas the difference in gender equality awareness remained significant. Interview participants attributed these differences to three factors, namely educational attainment and knowledge structure, exposure to media and information technology, and changes in social environment and family structure. Discussion Cohort membership in this workforce was closely intertwined with tenure, job level, and educational composition. The findings extend gender consciousness research, previously concentrated in media, education, and general labor market settings, into the hospitality workforce, and they suggest that uniform human resource policies may serve this workforce poorly. Practical implications include transparent promotion criteria, gender-neutral job design, and needs-responsive gender-awareness initiatives aimed at supporting female employees across different career circumstances.

This study aimed to develop nail art designs inspired by natural fractal motifs and compare the visual expression of DALL·E, Midjourney, and Stable Diffusion. Four natural fractal motifs were selected through a literature review: clouds, lightning, ant nests, and planets. A shared prompt framework incorporating fractal characteristics, formative elements, and nail art design requirements was established. Common English prompts were used as initial inputs for the three models, followed by image refinement using their respective functions. A focus group interview (FGI) with ten nail art professionals and instructors was conducted to examine design suitability and practical applicability. The generated images exhibited differences in composition, color, texture, and detail. FGI participants highlighted Midjourney’s representation of fractal elements, color harmony, texture rendering, and overall design quality. Their feedback informed the selection of Midjourney for physical artwork development. Four nail art works were produced, incorporating randomness and overlapping, nonlinearity and diffusion, irregularity and distortion, and an artistic interpretation of self-similarity and repetition. The visual features of the generated images were adapted to the materials and techniques used in physical production. This study presents a design development process integrating motif analysis, prompt design, image generation, FGI, and physical production. The findings suggest that generative AI can support the exploration of fractal-inspired nail art and offer a foundation for further applications in beauty design and education.

After the rapid development of generative large language models, the boundary involved in human and AI texts has become increasingly blurred, and academic integrity and intellectual property issues therefore need to be reconsidered. At present, many studies focus on automatic identification methods from the perspective of surface linguistic features, while they give limited explanation of the deep cognitive and neural phenomena involved when humans process the two types of texts. The present study combines computational linguistics, behavioral experiments, and neurocognition for examination, and makes a detailed analysis with electroencephalography (EEG) and eye-movement synchronization as the basic approach. The paper first summarizes the stable differences between human and AI texts in syntax, semantics, pragmatics, and other aspects, then discusses behavioral or eye-movement performance according to processing depth. It then interprets the N400, P600, and late positive component observed in fixation-related potentials as neural markers, and finally considers the relationship between factors such as genre and current research. The paper analyzes the key problem of the absence of whole-chain evidence for “linguistic features - neural responses,” and also proposes future directions such as sample expansion and cognition-guided detection. The framework proposed here has theoretical significance for AI text identification and the naturalness of large models.

With the rapid development of generative artificial intelligence, AI lyric generation tools such as Suno, Baidu Wenxin Lyric Generator, and Doubao have been widely deployed. However, AI-generated lyrics commonly suffer from thematic deviation, emotional fragmentation, stylistic mismatch, grammatical inconsistency, and long-structure logical collapse, making objective quality evaluation a critical link for optimizing generation models and filtering outputs. This paper systematically reviews existing research on AI-generated lyric quality evaluation along three main lines: evaluation dimensions, datasets, and technical routes. Existing approaches are categorized into four technical routes: manual subjective evaluation, traditional statistical and rule-based modeling, deep learning and representation learning, and large language model and multimodal intelligent evaluation. A three-layer progressive evaluation indicator system is constructed, comprising the textual language layer, lyric-music layer, and artistic aesthetic layer. The findings reveal four key bottlenecks: the deep gap between automatic quantitative metrics and human subjective aesthetic experience, the modeling blind spot for Chinese phonological features and lyric-music coordination, the severe scarcity of dedicated annotated datasets with uneven cultural distribution, and the disconnect between static text quality evaluation and dynamic human-computer collaboration experience. Future research should advance in three directions: developing lyric-specific vertical large models integrating music theory, constructing audio-text cross-modal joint lyric-music evaluation systems, and building generation-evaluation-optimization closed-loop ecosystems for the entire creative workflow.

The growing number of Internet of things (IoT) devices has dramatically expanded the scope of attack to which cybercriminals utilize it, and network security became a core issue of research and design. Honeypots-systems purposely made to attract and analyze attackers have been of invaluable use in monitoring and learning about the various threats on the IoT infrastructure. The current survey summarizes and discusses cur-rent developments in IoT honeypot technologies with particular focus on artificial intelligence, machine learning, and blockchain as game changers. Major issues addressed are high-interaction and low-interaction honeypot models, dynmaic transformation of ordinary IoT node to a honeypot during attack, and advantages of secure and tamper-resistant logging with blockchain. The paper explains how methods like reinforcement learning and deep neural networks have made honeypots adapt to attackers to identify anomalies in real time and gather more data to identify threats. Computational resource, automation and large-scale implementation-al constraints are also addressed as well as potential prospects to create more approachable, resistant honeypot systems. The presented work is intended to inform the future research and suggest strong security practices in the rapidly changing IoT environment by comparing the methods of the major scholarly studies and implementations.

Abstract The rapid migration of electrical grids towards Smart Grid (SG) architectures produces high-dimensional data streams that must be processed intelligently in real time. Traditional modelling, optimisation, and control approaches cannot handle the growing complexity of contemporary power systems. This comprehensive study aims to provide a synopsis of AI applications in smart grid settings for load forecasting, transient and voltage stability analysis, fault detection, and cybersecurity. This work provides a unified analytical framework that links supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, and ensemble learning techniques to specific smart grid operational problems, in contrast to prior surveys that address these areas separately. The main contributions are (i) a structured AI-smart grid functional taxonomy; (ii) critical analysis of the challenges of data quality, model interpretability, computational scalability and adversarial security; and (iii) a roadmap for explainable, reliable and carbon-neutral intelligent energy systems. Compared with more conventional methods, AI-based solutions often outperform them in prediction accuracy, stability, categorisation speed, and defect identification accuracy. However, there are major challenges in real-world deployment, standardisation and regulatory compliance.

Hurricanes are among the most destructive natural hazards. Effective risk communication through hurricane hazard maps is essential for reducing vulnerability to hazards. This paper examines how the public comprehends the design elements of risk category systems (colors, labels, and numbers of threat levels) in hazard maps through a systematic literature review and translates this evidence into recommendations for hurricane hazard map design. From an initial pool of 706 articles, 16 studies were selected for analysis. Key findings indicate that sequential color palettes such as yellow-to-red are preferred over rainbow schemes, that five to seven discrete risk classes support comprehension without overloading users, and that redundant encoding through labels and direct annotations improves accessibility for users with color vision deficiency. Findings provide insights for improving hurricane hazard map design and enhancing the communication of actionable hazard information.

documents.abstract: This study examines the causes, consequences, and mitigation strategies of academic hallucinations in the age of artificial intelligence. A mixed-methods research design is used, combining a survey of university lecturers, postgraduate students, and researchers with in-depth interviews involving journal editors, librarians, and AI experts. Quantitative data are analyzed using descriptive statistics, while qualitative data are subjected to thematic analysis. The findings indicate that inadequate AI literacy, poor prompt design, overreliance on AI-generated content, and the absence of institutional guidelines are major causes of academic hallucinations. The study further reveals that hallucinations contribute to fabricated citations, misinformation, reduced research credibility, ethical concerns, and declining public trust in scholarly communication. The study identifies effective mitigation strategies, including AI literacy training, prompt engineering, mandatory human verification, institutional AI policies, and the integration of AI detection and reference verification tools into academic workflows. The study contributes to the growing literature on responsible AI by proposing an integrated framework for minimizing academic hallucinations and strengthening research integrity. The findings provide practical recommendations for universities, researchers, publishers, and policymakers seeking to promote trustworthy and ethical AI-assisted academic research.

documents.abstract: Abstract This paper analyses the teaching and learning of academic communication through the lenses of posthumanism and distributed cognition and language. This is not intended as a solely philosophical exercise, but an attempt to map the factors and actants at play in the processes of learning and teaching to communicate in academic contexts. While emergent technologies, such as generative artificial intelligence, make this discussion particularly timely, I suggest that an expanded, embodied lens has always been necessary to understand how students learn to communicate, how they develop knowledge, and how they are socialised into academic disciplinary communities.

Purpose Digital therapeutics (DTx) are an emerging class of digital health innovation, increasingly recognized as critical for improving healthcare delivery, patient outcomes and sustainable health systems. Despite promising benefits, health care organizations are yet to realize the full benefits of DTx. Several factors influence the adoption of DTx within health information technology (HIT) ecosystems in emerging economies, such as India. From a strategic and system-level perspective, identification and prioritization of these factors is crucial to maximize their practical impact, given that some factors have more significant impact on outcomes than others. This exploratory study aims to identify and prioritize the enablers of DTx adoption for diabetes care in India. Design/methodology/approach The study adopted a sequential mixed-methods approach involving multiple stakeholders across two phases. Phase 1 involved in-depth semi-structured interviews with domain experts followed by inductive thematic analysis to explore the enablers of DTx adoption. Phase 2 prioritized these enablers using the best-worst method (BWM), based on expert judgment to inform decision-making. The robustness of the ranking was assessed using sensitivity analysis. Findings Qualitative analysis reveals 20 enablers of DTx adoption, which were broadly aligned with the dimensions of the human–organizational–technology–environmental (HOTE) framework. Quantitative analysis using BWM revealed the dominance of human-centric enablers, followed by organizational, environmental and technology-focused enablers. In particular, human enablers such as “Training for healthcare professionals” and “Patient education and engagement” emerged as the most influential enablers. Practical implications The findings offer practical, decision-supported insights based on expert-ranked enablers of DTx adoption, which is fundamentally a sociotechnical challenge that requires coordinated efforts across stakeholders to strengthen human capabilities, organizational readiness and secure data-sharing platforms. The results highlight the need for strong human engagement, leadership support and clear, enabling implementation regulations to facilitate DTx adoption. Originality/value The study provides a context-specific exploratory prioritization of the enablers of DTx adoption in emerging economies, such as India. The findings are based on expert judgment and offer initial decision-support guidance for practitioners and policymakers to accelerate digital health innovations adoption within HIT ecosystems.

Technology is playing a vital role across various sectors like education, healthcare, agriculture, financial services, employment, governance, and social development. However, we still see significant digital inequalities, especially in underserved communities, particularly in rural and low-income areas. Here, challenges such as limited connectivity, high technology costs, lack of digital skills, language barriers, and inaccessible digital services hinder meaningful participation in the digital economy. This conceptual paper delves into how adaptive Artificial Intelligence (AI) models can boost digital inclusion and support sustainable development in these communities. It brings together insights from literature on artificial intelligence, digital inclusion, adaptive learning, responsible AI, and sustainable development. The paper introduces the Adaptive AI Digital Inclusion and Sustainable Development (AIDISD) framework, which is built around five key dimensions: accessibility, personalization, contextual adaptation, resource efficiency, and community empowerment. It explores potential applications in education, healthcare, agriculture, financial inclusion, employment, and public services. Additionally, the paper highlights challenges related to infrastructure, data scarcity, algorithmic bias, privacy, cybersecurity, affordability, digital literacy, and institutional capacity. The analysis emphasizes that adaptive AI should be viewed as part of a larger socio-technical strategy rather than just a standalone tech solution. For inclusive deployment, we need local participation, suitable infrastructure, responsible data governance, human oversight, and ongoing evaluation. Ultimately, the paper concludes that well-designed adaptive AI systems can foster more inclusive and sustainable digital ecosystems, provided they are affordable, locally relevant, accessible, transparent, and aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals.
