documents.abstract: [English]: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence challenges traditional higher education curriculum management models that rely on rigid 4-to-5-year review cycles. This article aims to reformulate curriculum governance to become more adaptive in the AI era. Through a systematic integrative review of studies on higher education curriculum governance and AI adaptation from 2024 to 2026, a pressing need to shift from static to dynamic structures was identified. To address this mismatch, the article proposes the Adaptive Higher Education Curriculum (AHEC) framework, which strategically divides curriculum components into stable macro-level foundations and rapidly renewable micro-level contents. The findings reveal that modern curriculum governance must leverage AI-based Continuous Curriculum Intelligence to monitor shifts in professional competencies and job market requirements in real time. Crucially, the framework enforces human-centered authority, ensuring that human educators retain ultimate responsibility for final decision-making. The article concludes that agile managerial governance and organic institutional self-renewal are essential keys to ensuring that higher education programs maintain long-term professional relevance in an AI-mediated society. [Indonesian]: Perkembangan pesat kecerdasan buatan (AI), terutama AI generatif, menantang model manajemen kurikulum tradisional di perguruan tinggi yang biasanya mengandalkan siklus peninjauan berkala setiap 4 hingga 5 tahun. Artikel ini bertujuan untuk merumuskan ulang tata kelola dan manajemen kurikulum agar menjadi lebih adaptif di era AI. Melalui metode analisis konseptual berbasis integrative systematic review terhadap studi tata kelola kurikulum perguruan tinggi dan adaptasi AI dari tahun 2024 hingga 2026, ditemukan adanya kebutuhan mendesak untuk bergeser dari struktur kurikulum statis ke dinamis. Artikel ini menawarkan kerangka kerja Adaptive Higher Education Curriculum (AHEC) yang membagi komponen kurikulum menjadi lapisan stabil dan lapisan yang dapat diperbarui secara cepat. Hasil kajian menunjukkan bahwa manajemen kurikulum masa depan harus memanfaatkan Continuous Curriculum Intelligence berbasis AI untuk memantau perubahan kompetensi kerja secara waktu-nyata, namun keputusan akhir dan penafsiran maknanya tetap berada di bawah kendali penuh dosen dan institusi. Kesimpulan dari artikel ini menegaskan bahwa ketangkasan tata kelola manajerial merupakan kunci utama agar kurikulum perguruan tinggi tetap relevan dengan kebutuhan zaman harus jelas, ringkas, dan deskriptif.

The growing adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is transforming marketing education and increasing the need to understand the factors that drive its academic use among university students. This study aimed to analyze the determinants of GenAI adoption among university marketing students using the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2). A quantitative, explanatory, cross-sectional study was conducted with 310 marketing students from two Latin American universities in Peru and Costa Rica during the first academic semester of 2026. Participants were selected through non-probability purposive sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analyzed through Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS version 4.1.1.8. The findings indicate that habit is the main determinant of both behavioral intention and actual use of GenAI tools, while hedonic motivation, facilitating conditions, and price value also show significant positive effects. Conversely, performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and social influence do not significantly influence behavioral intention. It is concluded that the adoption of GenAI among university marketing students is increasingly driven by habitual academic use rather than by traditional technology acceptance factors. These findings provide evidence to support institutional strategies for the responsible integration of GenAI into higher education.

Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common clinical syndrome in the intensive care unit (ICU) that not only substantially increases in-hospital mortality but is also closely associated with the development and progression of chronic kidney disease, posing a serious threat to patient health. Recently, driven by advances in cutting-edge technologies such as liquid biopsy, multi-omics, and artificial intelligence, clinical research on AKI has achieved important breakthroughs. This narrative review systematically searched PubMed, Web of Science, EMBASE, and Cochrane Library databases for clinical studies published between January 2025 and August 2026, with particular emphasis on ICU-related AKI, especially surgery- and sepsis-associated AKI. The review focuses on three major aspects: early identification and risk stratification, optimization of prevention and treatment strategies, and individualized implementation and management of kidney replacement therapy. Between 2025 and 2026, clinical research on AKI yielded several important advances. These include the identification of multi-omics-based liquid-biopsy biomarkers and the development of causal deep-learning models enabling more accurate risk prediction. Terlipressin treatment improved reversal rates in selected patients with hepatorenal syndrome. However, multiple high-quality perioperative randomized controlled trials investigating blood pressure targets, artificial intelligence–assisted hemodynamic optimization, albumin infusion, and other interventions yielded negative or even harmful results, suggesting that hemodynamic interventions may have reached a benefit ceiling within current treatment paradigms. Meanwhile, the timing of kidney replacement therapy initiation, technical considerations, and weaning strategies have become increasingly customized. This review aims to provide the latest evidence-based information to guide clinical practice while identifying gaps in the current evidence and highlighting priorities for future research.

Deciphering early human embryonic development and organogenesis is constrained by limited access to in vivo specimens and the intrinsic complexity of spatiotemporal cell fate dynamics. Recent advances in spatiotemporal multi-omics have begun to overcome these barriers by enabling the reconstruction of in silico human embryos and developmental trajectories with spatial and temporal resolution. These approaches have revealed fundamental principles of lineage specification, cell migration, tissue morphogenesis, and axial patterning in early human development. In this Review, we summarize how single-cell and spatial multi-omics technologies, particularly spatial transcriptomics, have transformed the study of human early embryogenesis, organogenesis, and stem-cell-derived embryoid systems. We highlight analytical frameworks that integrate spatial context, temporal progression, and multimodal datasets, and discuss how biological discovery and algorithmic innovation have co-evolved. Finally, we outline how artificial intelligence, foundation models, and large-scale multimodal learning may eventually enable predictive and causal modeling of human development, while addressing current technical, interpretability, and ethical challenges.

Abstract Self-supervised learning (SSL) enables scalable, label-free foundation models (FMs) that learn task-agnostic representations directly from images, bypassing cell segmentation and feature engineering inherent to classical morphological profiling. We present a large-scale evaluation of SSL FMs for image-based phenotypic profiling, covering contrastive (DINO), masked-based generative (MAE, iTPN) and hybrid (DINOv2) learning mechanisms, pretrained on all unannotated chemical perturbations from the Joint Undertaking for Morphological Profiling–Cell Painting (JUMP–CP) dataset (119,876 compounds, ~1.77 million images, 7 laboratories). Here we show that top-performing SSL models outperformed CellProfiler in compound-replicate retrieval on the held-out JUMP–Target2 set (302 annotated compounds, P ≤ 0.001). DINO and DINOv2 generalized across diverse perturbations and cell types, outperforming CellProfiler with 31–37% gains in site-averaged mean average precision for mechanism-of-action retrieval on EU-OPENSCREEN Bioactives (2,464 compounds), and consistently surpassing masked-based models across all benchmarks. This study provides a systematic assessment of SSL approaches for advancing morphological profiling and offers pretrained FMs to accelerate drug discovery.

In 2014, the report A World That Counts, commissioned by the United Nations Secretary-General, argued that better access to high-quality data would improve public decision-making to address major global challenges more effectively (Independent Expert Advisory Group on a Data Revolution for Sustainable Development [IEAG], 2014). Since then, data availability has increased substantially, yet the corresponding benefits for public decision-making remain mixed (Fischer et al., 2025). If the difficulties political systems face in addressing contemporary problems persist despite this abundance, data availability cannot be the whole explanation. Policy processes and outcomes also depend on political pressures, institutional rules and interactions among policy actors, limited administrative capacity, and uncertainty about policy problems and their solutions (Howlett et al., 2015). These influences increasingly operate within complex systems, which may amplify the demands each of them creates (Fernández-i-Marín et al., 2024). We focus here on the cognitive processes through which policymakers interpret information, form judgments and make decisions under these demands. We define policymakers as individuals exercising decision-making responsibilities within governance systems, from the local to the supranational level. Following Cairney and Weible (2017) in viewing policymaking as imperfect cognition operating in complex contexts, we contend that the interaction between cognitive limits and rising systemic complexity is an important source of difficulty in policymakers' judgments and decisions. To support this thesis, we draw on research in complex systems, cognitive psychology and decision science, before examining how systems thinking, simulations and human-AI collaboration can help mitigate these limitations. We conclude by arguing for humility about what can be predicted and controlled in complex policy systems (Jalonen, 2025).Contemporary societies have become more complex as digitalization and globalization have deepened interdependencies among social, economic, and political spheres (Benbya et al., 2020;OECD, 2019). In such systems, interactions among actors generate unpredictable dynamics, limiting the ability of policymakers to anticipate how these systems evolve (Geyer & Rihani, 2010). The problems governments face are similarly complex: they evolve over time, emerge from multiple interactions, and involve actors with divergent interests. Their ambiguity leaves room for multiple interpretations, such that evidence alone is insufficient to determine what should be done (Cairney, 2019). At the global level, new governance arrangements have emerged to address such problems, including multi-stakeholder partnerships, adding another layer of institutional complexity (Elsässer et al., 2025). Yet responses of this kind can prove counterproductive, raising the risk of wicked solutions that leave decision-makers with a system more complex than before (Peters et al., 2019). Within national systems, policies accumulate (Adam et al., 2019), often faster than public administrations expand their capacity to implement them (Fernández-i-Marín et al., 2024), while policy texts themselves add complexity through demanding language and connections to other legal instruments (Senninger, 2023). Complexity is therefore not only a feature of the environment policymakers face, but is also amplified by the responses they devise.Decades of research on complex problem solving and dynamic decision-making document persistent difficulties in understanding complex, dynamic environments (Dörner & Funke, 2017;Osman, 2010). Following Béchard et al. (2025), we use the wall of complexity as a descriptive label for the substantial deterioration in judgment and decision performance that can occur when decision-makers confront highly complex tasks. It does not denote a single or fixed threshold. Although capacity limits have been quantified for specific processes such as working memory and relational reasoning, the extent of this deterioration depends on task characteristics, individual differences, the strategies used, and the external support available. Among the many ways complexity has been described, we retain the three dimensions that bear most directly on cognitive demand: computational, relational, and dynamic complexity.Computational complexity arises when the number of possible ways to solve a problem grows so rapidly that exhaustive consideration becomes infeasible (Hélie & Pizlo, 2022). In politics, we see this in the multiplicity of actors, objectives, and policy instruments that can be combined. Because working memory holds only a few items at a time (Cowan, 2010), decision-makers can consider only a fraction of these possibilities.Relational complexity reflects how many interdependent variables must be integrated simultaneously to represent a problem (Halford et al., 1998). Performance drops substantially from three to four variables, and falls to chance level at five (Halford et al., 2005). Political decision-making routinely involves many more interacting elements, as governance networks connect numerous interdependent public, private, and nonprofit actors (Morçöl, 2023).Finally, dynamic complexity arises from feedback loops, time delays, and nonlinear relationships that shape how systems evolve (Sterman, 1994). Political decision-making reflects these dynamics, as choices made in one sphere of governance can alter decisions taken in another (Klijn & Snellen, 2009). Yet humans have particular difficulty understanding delayed feedback (Brehmer, 1992) and basic dynamic processes (Cronin et al., 2009).These forms of complexity impose demands that can exceed human cognitive capacities. How cognition adapts to them is therefore central to understanding political decision-making.Whether policymakers can escape the wall of complexity depends on a prior question: are they cognitively better equipped to withstand it than ordinary citizens (Béchard et al., 2025)? Although political science has often treated political elites as cognitively distinct from the public (Kertzer, 2022), experimental comparisons reveal few systematic differences in how elected officials and citizens process information and make judgments (Griffin, 2013;Vis & Stolwijk, 2022). This question also extends to the organizations in which policymakers work. Such organizations can increase their information-processing capacity by delegating routine matters to specialized units, allowing multiple issues to be handled in parallel. When a problem cannot be adequately addressed through established procedures, however, it requires central coordination and a sequential search for alternatives, making the limits of individual cognition more consequential (Jones, 2003).Organizations can therefore distribute and sometimes mitigate the demands of complexity, but they do not eliminate the human cognitive constraints associated with the wall. Political decision-making thus remains cognitively bounded (Cairney, 2019), requiring policymakers to simplify what they attend to, represent, and reason about.Policymakers face chronic information overload that exceeds what they can process (Walgrave & Dejaeghere, 2017). Since attention is a limited resource, they must allocate it selectively, focusing on a few problems at a time (Baumgartner et al., 2023). Part of this selection is delegated to staff, while the rest relies on heuristics that filter what merits processing (Walgrave & Dejaeghere, 2017). What fails this first filter never reaches the later stages of the decision-making process. Such filtering can also have representational consequences, making some interests more cognitively accessible than others and leaving decision-makers with an incomplete picture of those affected (Miler, 2009). Nor is what passes the filter necessarily represented accurately. Even when a problem is noticed, its severity may be underestimated. When deterioration occurs through small, routine changes, the reference point for judging the problem may gradually adjust, making its cumulative severity appear less urgent -a boiling frog dynamic that Epp and Thomas (2023) associate with slower policy responses.Mental models organize incoming information by selecting the variables and causal relationships deemed relevant, but tend to neglect accumulations, delays, feedback, and nonlinearities (Sterman, 1994). They further reduce complexity by grouping elements into larger units or processing them sequentially (Halford et al., 1998), so reasoning ultimately operates on a simplified representation rather than the full problem (Hélie & Pizlo, 2022).While simplification is useful for making complex tasks more tractable, it can also produce systematic errors in judgment (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). Experimental evidence suggests that elected office does not insulate decision-makers from these errors. In a three-country study, elected representatives were strongly affected by gain-loss framing and status-quo presentation, and were more likely than citizens to continue investing in a failing program after substantial prior expenditure (Sheffer et al., 2018). Local councillors are similarly prone to conjunction errors and scope neglect (Stolwijk & Vis, 2021). Yet what matters for the quality of political decision-making is less the occurrence of these errors than the resistance of these errors to correction. Individuals readily detect distortions in the reasoning of others while judging their own conclusions to be sound (Pronin et al., 2002). Among politicians, additional evidence does not reduce, and can even increase, the influence of prior attitudes on how information is interpreted (Baekgaard et al., 2019). Requiring them to justify a decision has similar effect, strengthening motivated reasoning rather than tempering it (Christensen & Moynihan, 2024). Expertise and experience appear to offer little protection against such biases (Stolwijk & Vis, 2021). Despite reporting greater political knowledge, elected officials did not outperform the general population in a complex political simulation (Béchard et al., 2025).As the cognitive limits discussed above are structural, they cannot be eliminated, nor can decisionmakers overcome their effects on their own. The challenge is therefore to equip them to navigate complexity more effectively despite these constraints. We examine three ways of doing so: training decision-makers to reason about complex systems (Section 5.1), extending their capacities through human-AI collaboration (Section 5.2), and cultivating epistemic and regulatory humility about the limits of their judgment and of policy itself (Section 5.3).A first step is to develop systems thinking by learning to reason about the overall structure of a system or problem rather than its isolated elements (Fischer & Gonzalez, 2016). In our view, this should include an explicit understanding of key mechanisms of complexity, such as feedback, delays, nonlinear effects, and emergence. Complexity thinking provides an analytical lens for recognizing the evolving and partly unpredictable nature of these systems, and the resulting limits of prediction and control (Geyer & Rihani, 2010). The aim should be to foster what Funke (2022) calls complex systems literacy. Yet the dynamics of complex systems are often too counterintuitive to be inferred through unaided reasoning (Sterman, 2002). Merely thinking and talking about systems may therefore do little to reshape the mental models underlying decision-making, emphasizing the need for active modeling (Forrester, 2016). Although empirical evidence suggests that modelling used as a cognitive tool combined with explicit systems-thinking instruction can improve systems thinking (Hung, 2008), routinely building such models may be impractical for policymakers. We therefore see microworld simulations as a more accessible route to experiential training. These computerized environments incorporate key characteristics of complex systems while allowing participants to experiment with strategies and observe their consequences, without having to build the models themselves (Brehmer & Dörner, 1993). Microworlds have long been used to study complex and dynamic decision-making (Gonzalez et al., 2005), including in simulated governance environments, such as Ecopolicy (Lafond et al., 2012), and Democracy 3 (Béchard et al., 2025;Lafond et al., 2014).We see this as a promising foundation for extending their use to the training of policymakers. However, the effectiveness of such training depends on how the microworld is used rather than exposure alone (Sterman, 1994). Decision-making performance improves when training favours fewer, longer practice episodes over a greater number of short repetitions (Gonzalez, 2004), and when participants observe how an expert handles the task rather than reviewing their own decisions (Gonzalez, 2005). These findings, however, come from laboratory studies with university students, and whether skills acquired in microworlds transfer to real policy decisions remains to be established. And even if they do, training, however well designed, can change how a decision-maker approaches a system, but not eliminate the cognitive limits that constrain what they can process. That asymmetry is where tools designed to support decision-making become worth considering.Training can improve how decision-makers reason about complexity, but unaided cognition still has limits. A complementary approach is therefore to externalize part of the cognitive burden through decision-support technologies. Such tools can function as "cognitive prostheses," offloading part of the information-processing and representation demands onto external systems (Tremblay et al., 2017). AI considerably expands the possibilities for such cognitive support, not by providing decision-makers with more information, but by increasing their capacity to process and act upon it. It can support routine, information-intensive policy analysis (Wellstead et al., 2024), transform large volumes of raw data into decision-relevant information (Madanchian et al., 2026), and extend policy modelling by allowing decision-makers to test interventions before implementation (Margetts, 2022). Yet such cognitive support comes with a trade-off: the systems that help decision-makers navigate complexity can also shape how that complexity is perceived and judged. Algorithmic risk assessments, for example, can recast fundamental uncertainty as statistical risk (Hartmann & Wenzelburger, 2021), while AI-generated recommendations can become anchors for subsequent human judgments (Carter & Liu, 2025). More generally, cognitive vulnerabilities change with the degree of automation in the decision-making system: as human involvement decreases, risks shift from biases in human judgment toward excessive trust in the system and disengagement from the decision-making process (Van Rooy, 2024). These vulnerabilities mean that adding AI to human decision-making does not automatically lead to better decisions. Depending on how it is used and implemented, AI may mitigate some biases while reinforcing or creating others (Bertrand et al., 2022;Kliegr et al., 2021). AI may also relocate part of this complexity rather than reduce it, since machine-learning systems derive their outputs from high-dimensional computations that do not readily translate into humanly interpretable reasons (Burrell, 2016). Decision-makers who rely on systems they cannot fully understand can find it harder to answer for the decisions those systems inform, a difficulty that Grimmelikhuijsen and Meijer (2022) count among the threats to the legitimacy of algorithmic decision-making in government. We argue that these risks are not a reason to reject cognitive offloading, but to design human-AI collaboration more carefully. The challenge is therefore not to maximize AI involvement, but to design for complementarity between human and artificial cognition (Tremblay et al., 2026). Decision-support systems should make the goals, assumptions and uncertainties behind their recommendations intelligible to decision-makers, and allow these recommendations to be audited (Grisogono, 2020). This also requires AI systems specifically developed for public-policy contexts (Henderson et al., 2022), explicit allocations of human and algorithmic roles and degrees of autonomy (Simmler and Frischknecht, 2021), and anticipation of the organizational disruptions their implementation within governments creates (Tangi et al., 2025). Conceived in this way, human-AI collaboration could expand the ability of policymakers to navigate complexity beyond their natural capabilities, without replacing the judgment necessary for decision-making.There are several approaches to support human cognition; some are applied upstream, such as the development of systems thinking or the use of computer simulations, while others, such as AI, can enhance the decision-support tools used during the decision-making process itself. But these tools alone will not suffice, because training to deal with complexity involves not only acquiring new tools but also developing a certain form of epistemic humility. First and foremost, it involves recognizing that decision-making biases exist, that they have structural origins (Korteling et al., 2020), and that they influence our judgment even when we are aware of them (Pronin & Kugler, 2007). The next step is to be aware of the vulnerability of unaided human cognition in the face of complexity, and the need for support beyond individual effort alone. Jalonen's (2025) review recommends a humble approach, by recognizing that the properties of complex political-administrative systems make their evolution inherently difficult to predict and control. This mindset can be learned. Dunlop and Radaelli (2016) propose training practitioners in what they call regulatory humility, that is, questioning the limits of what can be regulated, recognizing that certain situations are partly beyond the control of public policy, and confronting their own illusions of control. Making policymakers aware of what, amid complexity, will always remain beyond their control is not an admission of powerlessness: it is the prerequisite for working around the wall rather than running into it.Political systems are becoming more complex. Under high complexity, the natural capacities of human cognition may no longer be sufficient for effective judgment and decision-making. Faced with this wall, policymakers adapt the way they process information by simplifying reality. Heuristics are a natural response, but they can also become a source of bias and errors in judgment. Suboptimal political decisions are therefore not necessarily a sign of individual incompetence but may also reflect cognitive mechanisms that reach their limits when confronted with high levels of complexity.We posit that the interaction between the universal limits of human cognition and the complexity of the contexts in which this cognition operates (Cairney & Weible, 2017) is an important, often overlooked, source of difficulty in political decision-making. We have proposed three complementary responses to this difficulty: developing systems thinking through training and simulations, extending decision-making capacity through human-AI collaboration, and cultivating the epistemic and regulatory humility needed to use both well. None of these responses removes the cognitive limits of policymakers, but together they can help them navigate complexity more effectively.

Many university students come from equity and diverse backgrounds; they often balance study with employment, caregiving, and health challenges. This chapter considers how students from equity backgrounds engage with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). It draws on interview data, constructed as vignettes, and employs Emirbayer and Mische’s conception of practical-evaluative agency to explore how GenAI opens (or narrows) new trajectories of action for students. The analysis revealed that GenAI created options that were previously unavailable or misaligned with the students’ values or their perceived expectations. Their choices to engage with GenAI tools were typically oriented towards making progress under pressure. For students undertaking assessment tasks online and largely alone, GenAI operates as a mediating resource that provides rapid access to otherwise hidden or implicit information and offers immediate assistance with tasks. From this perspective, GenAI functions as an enabler of action in the moment. However, it may bypass interactions that contribute to learning and belonging. Rather than viewing GenAI use as inherently enabling or sacrificing, it may be more appropriate to see it as redistributing agency across time: expanding what is possible in the pressured present, while reshaping what is possible over longer timescales.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Agent Scrum keeps Scrum's core devices (a time-boxed sprint, a committed sprint backlog, story points, velocity, a Definition of Done and a retrospective) and rescales them for teams of AI coding agents. Sprints last two hours instead of two weeks; capacity comes from model rate limits instead of headcount; cost is measured as token velocity, the tokens consumed per merged story point. In the reference implementation, 79% of committed stories reached done inside the sprint (297 of 375 over 90 sprints), ceremony took under five minutes per sprint, and the human stakeholder spent under two hours a day. Working paper, version 0.1.

The shift of large language models (LLMs) from passive text generators to agentic systems marks a move toward autonomous intelligence. Agentic AI refers to systems that reason, plan, and execute actions in pursuit of complex goals with minimal human intervention. This paper reviews recent research on the architectural foundations, core functional modules, applications, and safety challenges of autonomous LLM systems. Current work emphasizes modular architectures in which an LLM serves as the central reasoning engine, augmented by components for perception, memory, planning, and tool interaction. Multi-agent systems have emerged as a dominant trend, enabling collaborative problem solving through structured orchestration and communication protocols. Although these systems show significant potential in software engineering, manufacturing, and cybersecurity, critical barriers remain in safety, reliability, and ethical governance. This review provides a structured overview of the state of the art and identifies key research directions for the coming years. Index Terms—agentic AI, autonomous agents, large language models, multi-agent systems, retrieval-augmented generation, tool use, AI safety

Artificial intelligence is transforming assistive technologies, yet many systems remain reactive, fragmented, and insufficiently personalized for individuals with disabilities and neurodivergent conditions. This chapter examines the architectural, design, and governance foundations of trustworthy agentic assistive systems. It synthesizes limitations of conventional approaches, including restricted adaptability, low interoperability, and weak support for user autonomy, and introduces a taxonomy of agentic architectures to guide scalable deployment. The chapter proposes a multi-agent framework integrating multimodal interaction, hybrid reasoning, explainable AI, and health-aware data to enable context-sensitive support. It further addresses privacy, ethical governance, and responsible institutional adoption while outlining future research directions. By bridging architectural innovation with human-centered design, this work advances a forward-looking vision for inclusive intelligent environments.

documents.abstract: This chapter examines agentic IoT as an emerging paradigm for renewable energy integration in smart cities. Conventional IoT architectures have improved urban energy monitoring and connectivity but remain largely reactive and rule-bound, insufficient for the coordination demands of distributed generation, intermittent supply, electrified mobility, and heterogeneous urban infrastructure. The chapter defines agentic IoT as an urban energy ecosystem in which connected devices, edge nodes, and digital platforms are embedded with situational awareness, dynamic decision-making, multi-agent coordination, adaptive learning, and bounded autonomous execution within predefined safety and policy constraints. A multi-layer conceptual framework is proposed, organized around physical energy assets, IoT sensing and actuation, data and digital twin capabilities, agentic intelligence, platform and ecosystem integration, and governance. The framework positions agentic IoT as an evolution beyond conventional and intelligent IoT toward more autonomous urban energy orchestration.

Artificial intelligence (AI) and immersive technologies are expanding opportunities for language learners to obtain feedback, revise writing, and rehearse communication. Their educational value depends on how these opportunities support learning and informed participation. Wu et al. (2025) locate recent technological developments within broader concerns about learner affect, teacher development, and immersive learning. This wider perspective is useful for understanding the nine articles in this special issue. Together, they examine how technological assistance interacts with critical thinking, authorship, communicative practice, and teacher agency. We bring these contributions into dialogue to consider the pedagogical conditions under which innovation supports learners’ developing capabilities.

Smart grid systems have been utilized with artificial intelligence (AI) which has substantially improved their efficiency and reliability. Nevertheless, with the development of smart grids into more intricate, networked, and data-intensive systems, a smart grid is becoming more susceptible to cybercrime. The chapter handles the problem of cybersecurity available within smart grid systems shedding light on the especial vulnerabilities that lies in the fact that they are digital and automated. It talks about the application of AI-based solutions to deal with such risks and it focuses on approaches that include anomaly detection, real-time threat responsiveness, and forecast risk. Besides, the chapter is also about AI aimed at protecting the communication network and providing more effective identification processes, and autonomic safe work. Through interpretation of case studies and projections in the real world, this paper gives a holistic idea of how AI can enhance the cybersecurity infrastructure in smart grid infrastructures.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly becoming part of the knowledge infrastructure of healthcare. From diagnostic support and image interpretation to patient communication and clinical decision-making, AI-supported technologies, including generative AI, are changing the conditions under which healthcare professionals work. Dentistry is no exception. Recent research highlights emerging applications of AI in dental practice, while international reviews suggest growing opportunities and challenges associated with integrating AI into dental education. However, the rapid development of AI-supported technologies raises questions about how effectively professional education and continuing professional development can respond to evolving competency requirements. This raises a central question: How can dental education and continuing professional development respond to the potential double competence gap associated with AI-enabled dental practice?In this Opinion article, we address this question by proposing a conceptual framework that distinguishes between an initial education-practice gap and a continuing professional competence gap. Drawing on the concepts of AI literacy, Professional Digital Competence, and symbiotic intelligence, we discuss how dental education may develop and assess the competencies required for critical, ethical, and responsible AI use while preserving independent clinical reasoning, professional accountability, and patient-centred care.The rapid development of artificial intelligence raises important questions about how dental education can maintain the relevance of its curricula while safeguarding established standards of clinical competence, patient safety, and professional accountability. Although international reviews indicate growing interest in AI applications within dental education, systematic curricular integration appears to vary across institutions and educational contexts (9,10,24). Such variation should not necessarily be interpreted as resistance to technological change, as cautious implementation may also reflect legitimate concerns about educational quality, clinical validity, ethical safeguards, and the availability of robust evidence. Preliminary analyses of regulations and national curriculum frameworks for professional education raise questions about whether current educational provision adequately addresses emerging AIrelated competency requirements, potentially contributing to the two dimensions of the proposed double competence gap. Preliminary analyses of regulations and national curriculum frameworks for professional education suggest that this may contribute to reinforcing an already existing double competence gap When generative artificial intelligence became widely accessible through platform-based services such as ChatGPT in the autumn of 2022, many assumed that it would primarily affect the technology sector. However, when we tested a professional version of ChatGPT (GPT-4) in medicine, and partly in dental and psychology education, in March 2023, it was already apparent that this represented a technological paradigm shift with potentially farreaching implications across professional education programmes (1,2).While AI capabilities have developed rapidly in recent years in the health sciences (3)(4)(5)(6)(7)(8)(9)(10)(11), their integration into dental education presents a different set of challenges. Curriculum development, faculty preparation, assessment design, and clinical governance require careful consideration and cannot necessarily follow the pace of technological innovation. Recent reviews indicate that AI-related educational initiatives are emerging, but their integration into formal curricula and assessment practices remains variable. Several key explanations emerge from the literature: already overcrowded curricula, insufficient profession-specific digital competence among educators, and a lack of structured implementation (9,10,24). This potential misalignment between technological developments and structured educational provision provides an important rationale for examining the proposed double competence gap.Dental education has previously incorporated technologies such as digital radiography, simulation, intraoral scanning, and computer-aided design and manufacturing (29). These developments offer relevant lessons for AI integration: new technologies require faculty development, opportunities for supervised practice, alignment with clinical tasks, and assessment of what students can actually do. However, the current AI transition differs in its breadth and pace. Generative AI can be used across clinical reasoning, communication, learning, and assessment, including through tools that students access independently of their institutions. Moreover, the capabilities and limitations of these systems may change within a single curriculum cycle. Dental programmes should therefore draw on established approaches to curricular implementation while developing a more continuous process for reviewing AIrelated learning outcomes, teaching cases, and assessment practices.The Norwegian national curriculum regulations for healthcare professional education (RETHOS) emphasise that educational programmes should respond to society's current and future competence needs. However, AI is not explicitly addressed in the national curriculum regulations for dentistry, medicine, or psychology (12)(13)(14). Similarly, the Norwegian Agency for Quality Assurance in Education (NOKUT)'s national evaluation of medical education in 2025 provides limited explicit discussion of AI (15). These observations should be interpreted with caution. The absence of explicit AI terminology in national regulations or evaluation reports does not necessarily imply that AIrelated competencies are absent from institutional curricula, teaching practices, or assessment arrangements. National frameworks may deliberately emphasise enduring, technology-neutral professional competencies, allowing educational institutions to adapt their programmes to technological developments without requiring frequent regulatory revisions.Nevertheless, the limited explicit attention to AI in these national documents raises relevant questions about how emerging AI-related competencies are interpreted, operationalised, and assessed within individual educational programmes. International reviews have identified variation in the integration of AI into dental education, including challenges related to curriculum development, faculty preparedness, and the assessment of AI-related competencies (9,10,24).From the perspective of the proposed double competence gap framework, the central concern is therefore not simply whether AI is explicitly mentioned in national policy documents, but whether educational programmes systematically develop and assess the competencies required for responsible AI use in dental practice. Addressing this question requires empirical examination of institutional curricula, learning outcomes, educational activities, and assessment practices rather than relying solely on national policy analysis.Although the policy examples discussed here are drawn from Norway, the distinction between national competency frameworks, institutional curricula, and actual educational practices may also be relevant internationally. However, the extent to which the proposed double competence gap applies across different countries and dental education systems requires context-specific empirical investigation.The increasing integration of AI into healthcare knowledge infrastructures may also have epistemological implications for professional education. As AI systems become involved in information retrieval, diagnostic support, and clinical decision-making, questions arise concerning how professional knowledge is produced, evaluated, interpreted, and applied. These developments may gradually reshape aspects of professional roles and clinical reasoning, although their scope, pace, and educational consequences remain uncertain. Rather than predicting a specific timeline for such changes, dental education should develop adaptable approaches that enable students and practising professionals to critically evaluate emerging technologies while maintaining established standards of clinical expertise and professional accountability (16,18). Professional digital competence and AI literacy should become integral components of both the knowledge infrastructure and professional competence, and conceptual frameworks need to be developed that account for professionspecific AI use across both urban and rural patient contexts (17).At the same time, the challenge extends far beyond today's dentist education. The vast majority of today's practising professionals completed their education long before generative artificial intelligence became part of professional practice. Consequently, they have not necessarily received systematic training in how such AI systems can be used professionally, what their limitations are, or which ethical and legal challenges they may entail.We propose the concept of a double competence gap to describe two distinct but interconnected potential mismatches between the competencies required for responsible professional practice in increasingly AI-enabled dental healthcare and the competencies systematically developed through initial dental education and continuing professional development. A competence gap is understood here as a discrepancy between demonstrable professional capabilities and the knowledge, skills, and critical judgement required to perform relevant professional tasks safely, effectively, and ethically. Importantly, such gaps cannot be inferred solely from the availability of new technologies or the absence of explicit AI terminology in educational policy documents; their existence and extent require empirical investigation.The first competence gap, which we term the initial education-practice gap, concerns the potential misalignment between undergraduate dental education and the evolving competencies required in AI-enabled dental practice. International reviews suggest that the systematic integration of AI-related learning outcomes, teaching activities, and assessment practices in dental education remains uneven (9,10,24). This raises questions about whether existing educational provision adequately prepares students for the critical and clinically appropriate use of AI in future dental practice. Although students may independently engage with generative AI and other AI-supported technologies, such engagement does not necessarily constitute systematic development of profession-specific AI literacy. The central educational concern is therefore whether curricula, learning outcomes, teaching practices, and assessment arrangements adequately prepare students to critically evaluate AI-generated information, recognise its limitations, and integrate appropriate AI-supported decisionmaking with established clinical knowledge and professional judgement.The second competence gap, termed the continuing professional competence gap, concerns practising dentists whose initial professional education preceded the widespread availability of contemporary generative AI and other emerging AI applications. These professionals may encounter new technological expectations without having had equivalent opportunities for structured education in AI evaluation, clinical applicability, patient safety, data protection, and professional accountability. However, the extent of this gap is likely to vary across practitioners, clinical settings, previous digital experience, and access to continuing professional development.The conceptual contribution of the double competence gap framework lies in connecting these two educational challenges across the professional life course. Whereas AI literacy describes a set of relevant competencies, and Professional Digital Competence provides a broader perspective on technology-related professional capabilities, the double competence gap framework draws attention to the potential misalignment between competency requirements and educational provision at two different stages of professional development. It thereby offers a basis for examining how initial education, curriculum and assessment, faculty development, and continuing professional development can respond to changing professional requirements.We present the double competence gap as a conceptual and empirically testable proposition rather than as an established finding across dental education. Its educational significance depends on whether these proposed mismatches can be identified, assessed, and addressed in specific institutional and professional contexts.Empirically investigating the proposed double competence gap requires distinguishing between shortcomings in educational provision and demonstrable deficiencies in professional competence. The initial education -practice gap could be examined through curriculum mapping, IADT-guidelines (34IADT, 2026), analysis of intended learning outcomes and assessment practices, interviews with educators and students, and performance-based assessments of AI-related clinical competencies. The continuing professional competence gap could be investigated through research informed knowledge (33e.g. Ji et al., 2025), surveys, interviews, and scenario-based assessments involving practising dentists with different levels of professional experience and AI exposure. Importantly, the absence of explicit AI-related learning outcomes or structured training would indicate a potential gap in educational provision, but would not, in itself, demonstrate insufficient professional competence. Establishing a competence gap would require comparing observable performance with independently defined, clinically relevant competency standards, while accounting for differences in professional roles, practice contexts, and access to continuing professional development.Addressing the proposed double competence gap requires conceptual clarity regarding AI literacy, Professional Digital Competence (PDC), and symbiotic intelligence (SI). Although these concepts are closely related, they represent distinct dimensions of professional competence and human -AI interaction in dental education and practice.AI literacy refers to the knowledge, skills, and critical judgement required to understand, evaluate, and appropriately use AI systems within specific professional contexts. documents.abstract: Online businesses must answer product questions, explain policies, guide purchases and resolve order-related concerns across multiplechannels. Human-only support can be costly and slow during peak demand, while rigid rule-based chatbots struggle with varied wording andmulti-step questions. This paper presents a conceptual design for an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Chat Assistant for Online Business thatcombines natural language understanding, retrieval from approved business knowledge, controlled access to commerce services andescalation to human staff. The proposed assistant interprets customer intent, retrieves relevant product and policy information, generatesgrounded responses, and invokes permitted actions such as checking order status only after appropriate authentication. The architectureemphasizes factual consistency, privacy, security, accessibility and measurable service quality. It also describes a developmentmethodology, evaluation metrics, risk controls and a staged deployment plan. Since this is a design-oriented study, no original performanceresults are claimed; the proposed evaluation must be conducted using representative customer queries and verified business data.

The instructional effectiveness of artificial intelligence (AI) dialogue tools in higher education varies across contexts and depends on multiple moderation mechanisms. This structured evidence synthesis of eight studies identifies four moderation dimensions: task embedding depth, feedback granularity, teacher orchestration intensity, and discipline verification pressure. These dimensions are examined through task cycles, feedback characteristics, teacher intervention, and verification requirements. The findings show that higher intensity configurations with structured task embedding, layered feedback, teacher orchestration, and content verification are associated with higher composite coding indices across learning gains, engagement, trust, and knowledge transfer. A four-stage closed-loop learning pathway is proposed to support the pedagogical integration of AI dialogue tools. The findings highlight the importance of moderation mechanisms, teacher orchestration, and feedback granularity in designing effective AI-supported learning environments.

documents.abstract: For this study, we first did an assessment of students’ motivation for HE and their academic experience so far; we then examined university students’ perceptions of the use Artificial Intelligence in their formal learning. The participants were students enrolled into different courses at Cosmopolitan university, Abuja. This research survey examines university students’ perceptions of the use Artificial Intelligence in their higher education learning. A descriptive survey research method was used. Specifically, a questionnaire was used to collect data. The participants were students enrolled in different courses at Cosmopolitan university in Abuja, Nigeria. The results showed that the participants had positive perceptions of the use Artificial Intelligence in their university learning in affective, cognitive, and cognitive domains. Students’ perceptions of the use Artificial Intelligence in their university learning did not differ significantly according to perceived digital dependency. However, students’ perceptions of the use Artificial Intelligence in their university learning were influenced by their use of some AI tools and perceived digital competency. Future directions based on the findings were presented

documents.abstract: This chapter explores the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), universal design for learning (UDL), and inclusive teaching practices in higher education to enhance institutional performance. It examines how AI supports personalised learning, accessibility, and differentiated instruction aligned with UDL principles. Using conceptual analysis, the chapter shows that inclusive teaching improves engagement, retention, and equitable outcomes. It also situates inclusive pedagogy within social justice frameworks. Findings indicate that AI strengthens flexibility and responsiveness, while UDL promotes proactive accessibility for diverse learners. However, challenges such as algorithmic bias, data privacy, and unequal access remain critical considerations.

ABSTRACT The increasing complexity of modern processors presents challenges for students in understanding the fundamental principles of computer architecture and digital logic design. Traditional microprocessors and microcontrollers often conceal their internal operations, making it difficult for learners to visualize how individual logic components work together to execute instructions.This study aims to develop an educational processor model that integrates Artificial Intelligence (AI) assistance with digital logic design to improve the understanding of processor architecture and instruction execution. The proposed system will utilize fundamental digital logic components, including logic gates, registers, an Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU), a control unit, a program counter, and memory, to demonstrate the basic operations of an 8-bit processor. AI assistance will be explored to support circuit design, logic analysis, instruction decoding, and troubleshooting during the development process. The processor will demonstrate the fetch–decode–execute cycle and basic arithmetic, logical, and data transfer operations through a practical and observable implementation. Functional testing and simulation will be used to verify the correctness of the processor's operations and the reliability of its component interconnections. By combining AI-assisted development with hands-on digital logic implementation, the study aims to provide a practical, accessible, and cost-effective educational resource for students studying computer engineering, digital electronics, and computer architecture. The proposed system is expected to bridge the gap between theoretical concepts and practical hardware implementation while encouraging critical thinking, problem-solving, and independent learning. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, 8-Bit Processor, Digital Logic Components, Computer Architecture, Educational Applications, Instruction Execution

Objectives The aim of the study was to identify and evaluate the possibilities of using artificial intelligence assistants to support decision-making processes related to asset allocation, treated as an important component of the business model of an enterprise operating under conditions of market uncertainty. Material and methods The study was conducted on the example of three companies from the construction sector listed on the Warsaw Stock Exchange: Budimex S.A., Polimex Mostostal S.A., and Mirbud S.A. The analysis covered the years 2020–2024 and was based on two groups of data: annual fundamental indicators and daily closing stock prices. In the fundamental part, return on equity, debt ratio, asset utilization ratio, and the Altman discriminant model were used to construct a synthetic fundamental index. In the market part, daily logarithmic rates of return and the Sharpe ratio were calculated. Results The results indicate that AI assistants can effectively support the analytical process by accelerating calculations and increasing the repeatability of the procedure. At the same time, differences in model performance were observed, indicating the risk of errors in data interpretation. Conclusions The study demonstrates that AI can be a useful tool supporting asset allocation management; however, its effectiveness depends on data quality, the precision of the analytical procedure, and human supervision. The findings highlight the importance of control mechanisms and model triangulation in AI-supported decision-making processes.

Introduction The rapid adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools for personalized learning in higher education has generated growing interest in their effects on student outcomes, yet comparative evidence remains limited. This systematic review and meta-analysis examined whether AI-based personalized learning is associated with differences in objectively measured academic performance, compared with instruction without the AI component, among higher education students. Methods Following PRISMA 2020, Scopus and Web of Science were searched in April 2026. Eligible studies implemented an AI system that adapted content, feedback, pacing or recommendations to learners, included a concurrent or historical comparator group, and reported an objective academic-performance outcome. Of 84 unique records, four controlled studies (420 students), all conducted in computing and engineering courses, met the criteria: one cluster-randomized study, one study reporting random allocation without procedural detail, one non-randomized study with a concurrent control, and one study with a historical control. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 or ROBINS-I, and certainty of evidence with GRADE. Results A random-effects model (REML) yielded a pooled Hedges' g of 1.01 (95% CI 0.33–1.68); with the Hartung-Knapp small-sample adjustment the interval widened to −0.10–2.11 and included no effect. Heterogeneity was substantial ( I 2 = 89%; τ 2 = 0.41), and the 95% prediction interval (−0.42–2.43) also included no effect. Leave-one-out estimates ranged from 0.80 to 1.22. Two studies were at serious risk of bias, and the certainty of evidence was very low. Discussion The available controlled studies suggest a potentially beneficial association between AI-based personalized learning and academic performance in computing and engineering courses, but the magnitude and consistency of this association remain uncertain, and causal conclusions are not warranted. Systematic Review Registration https://osf.io/amxpf/overview .

documents.abstract: Skin diseases are common, but seeing a dermatologist is not easy for everyone, especially in under-served regions. Many deep-learning classifiers are heavy, hard to interpret and stop at a class label. We present MediCare AI, a lightweight screening system that sorts skin images into seven disease categories by fully fine-tuning an ImageNet-pretrained ConvNeXt-Tiny with AdamW, cosine learning-rate decay, label smoothing and early stopping. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping shows which parts of the image drove each prediction. A Streamlit app accepts uploaded photos and live camera frames, reports the confidence and a rough three-level visible phase, and gives treatment suggestions and preventive advice through a generative service, with a local offline fallback. A single network reached roughly 80%–90% validation accuracy. The tool is meant for education and early screening, not as a replacement for professional diagnosis. Index Terms—skin disease classification, ConvNeXt, transfer learning, Grad-CAM, explainable artificial intelligence, Streamlit.

This research manuscript presents a proposed artificial intelligence-based approach for verifying tyre wear and tear using image classification and a MobileNet-based deep learning model. The objective is to explore how computer vision can support the identification of tyre wear conditions and assist vehicle maintenance and road-safety practices.The proposed workflow includes collecting tyre images, preparing and preprocessing the image dataset, training a MobileNet-based classification model, and evaluating its performance using appropriate classification metrics. The approach is intended to provide a foundation for a practical tyre inspection support system.The manuscript discusses the background, proposed methodology, potential applications, evaluation plan, limitations, and future scope of AI-based tyre wear detection. Reliable evaluation requires access to the original dataset, trained model, and test results. Since verified experimental results are not currently available, this manuscript does not claim a measured accuracy or experimentally validated performance.The work is relevant to automotive engineering, computer vision, deep learning, vehicle maintenance, and intelligent inspection systems.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia in the elderly. Traditional drugs targeting Aβ and Tau proteins face development bottlenecks. In recent years, studies have shown that NLRP3 inflammasome-mediated neuroinflammation in the brain is a key mechanism in the pathogenesis of AD. However, the number of existing NLRP3-specific inhibitors is limited, and they generally suffer from insufficient blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration. This study aims to combine artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning technologies to construct a multi-task screening model that can simultaneously predict the inhibitory activity of small molecule NLRP3 and its ability to penetrate the blood-brain barrier, providing an efficient and low-cost computational screening technology solution for the development of novel anti-inflammatory drugs for Alzheimer's disease. It uses AlphaFold to obtain target protein structures and combines them with the ZINC20/PubChem chemical database to construct a compound dataset. Using Python as the core tool, a random forest multi-task machine learning model was built using the Google Colab cloud platform. Physicochemical parameters such as molecular weight, lipid solubility (LogP), and polar surface area (TPSA) were selected as input features for the model. The drug’s NLRP3 activity and BBB penetration were used as the core prediction labels for model training and cross-validation. The model demonstrated high predictive performance in 5-fold cross-validation, with an average accuracy of 68.89% for predicting NLRP3 activity and an average accuracy of 97.78% for predicting blood-brain barrier penetration. Feature importance analysis confirmed that LogP and TPSA are the most critical physicochemical features that determine whether candidate molecules can penetrate the blood-brain barrier. Several candidate small molecules with both NLRP3 inhibition potential and BBB penetration were screened from a large-scale candidate molecule library. This study successfully constructed a low-cost, easy-to-implement AI-assisted drug screening system for neurological diseases, which can provide data support for the development of lead compounds for novel anti-inflammatory targeted drugs for Alzheimer's disease.

This chapter presents an artificial intelligence-driven battery health monitoring framework for sustainable electric vehicle applications. It discusses battery parameters including State of Charge, State of Health, degradation characteristics, and Remaining Useful Life together with data acquisition, preprocessing, feature extraction, and normalization techniques for battery health prediction. Machine learning approaches such as Random Forest, Artificial Neural Networks, and Long Short-Term Memory networks are reviewed for degradation analysis and predictive maintenance. An experimental case study demonstrates the effectiveness of the developed framework in accurately estimating battery states and tracking degradation behavior. The chapter also explores intelligent battery management, fault diagnosis, digital twins, smart grids, Internet of Things, and Vehicle-to-Grid integration for future energy systems.

Late and error-prone government accounts weaken legislative oversight and citizen scrutiny. This study examines whether documented adoption of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven data automation is associated with the timeliness and accuracy of financial reports in Nigeria's federal public sector. Using a ten-year balanced panel (2015–2024) of five purposively selected institutions, the Federal Ministry of Finance, the Office of the Accountant-General of the Federation, the Federal Inland Revenue Service, the Central Bank of Nigeria and the Bureau of Public Procurement, the study scores documentary evidence from annual reports, financial statements and official AI-implementation documents on a five-point (0–4) rubric and estimates pooled, fixed-effects, trend-adjusted, first-difference and lagged panel regressions, interpreted through agency theory. AI-driven data automation is positively and significantly associated with the composite measure of reporting timeliness and accuracy (pooled β = 0.717, R² = 0.845; within-institution β = 0.706, within R² = 0.818). The association remains positive and significant after controlling for a common time trend (β = 0.641), in first differences (β = 0.761) and when automation is lagged one year (β = 0.631). A one-point higher automation score is therefore associated with roughly 0.6 to 0.8 points higher reporting quality on the five-point scale. Because the design is observational, the measures are documentary indices, and the sample is small and purposively selected, the results indicate association rather than proven causation and are interpreted for the five institutions examined rather than for all federal ministries, departments and agencies. The findings support targeted investment in AI-enabled data capture, validation and reconciliation, accompanied by governance arrangements, human review and skills development.

Mothers caring for children with Autism Spectrum Disorder often face ongoing stress, emotional challenges, and significant caregiving responsibilities. These factors can affect family dynamics and the quality of support services available for disabilities. Although traditional counselling can offer some psychological relief, it may lack personalization, scalability, or ongoing monitoring. This chapter presents a mindfulness-based intervention enhanced by artificial intelligence, utilizing established techniques like Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction to provide flexible and accessible mental health resources. By combining AI with structured mindfulness practices, this approach seeks to improve emotional regulation, promote increased caregiver engagement, and foster better collaboration with disability service organizations. The chapter emphasizes that AI-enhanced mindfulness can serve as a valuable resource to bolster caregiver resilience and facilitate more efficient and responsive delivery of disability services.

The transition of artificial intelligence from unimodal learning systems to integrated multimedia and multimodal intelligence marks a critical shift in how machines perceive, reason, and interact with complex environments. Despite recent advances, current architectures remain constrained by computational scalability, limited contextual awareness, and indirect human–machine communication. This chapter explores future trajectories in AI-driven multimodal intelligence through the convergence of quantum artificial intelligence (QAI), brain–computer interfaces (BCIs), and next-generation deployment frameworks. The chapter adopts a conceptual research approach to examine how quantum-enhanced learning mechanisms can accelerate multimodal data fusion, optimize high-dimensional representations, and enable real-time cognitive analytics. In parallel, emerging BCI technologies are analyzed as transformative interfaces that integrate neural signals into intelligent systems, fostering adaptive environments responsive to human cognitive and emotional states. Together, these innovations signal a paradigm shift from algorithm-centric automation towards collaborative human–AI ecosystems. A phased roadmap is proposed, outlining foundational integration, cognitive expansion, and long-term human–machine symbiosis. Particular attention is given to developing economies, especially African contexts, where infrastructural constraints coexist with significant opportunities for leapfrogging through AI-enabled healthcare, education, logistics, and governance systems. Ethical governance, digital inclusion, workforce development, and data sovereignty are critically discussed as foundational pillars for sustainable deployment. The chapter concludes that responsible convergence across quantum computing, neurotechnology, and multimodal architectures supported by interdisciplinary collaboration and inclusive policy frameworks is essential for translating experimental innovations into scalable societal impact, positioning AI as a catalyst for equitable global development.

Smart assistants are evolving from exclusively voice-based interfaces to multimodal systems capable of seeing and hearing. This chapter explores how integrating vision and voice capabilities enables more intelligent and context-aware assistants, with a focus on industry use cases. We analyze the main areas of application where voice and vision integration is having a significant impact, from healthcare to retail and service robots, industrial maintenance, and automotive co-pilots. The chapter discusses the artificial intelligence techniques behind these systems, including multimodal deep learning models, sensor data fusion, and real-time decision-making, and addresses challenges such as synchronization, privacy, and user trust. Through the combination of voice and vision, the latest generation of smart assistants is breaking new ground in human–computer interaction.

Precision oncology is an approach in which cancer treatment is selected according to the molecular, genomic and clinical characteristics of an individual patient and tumour. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning, deep learning and natural language processing, can analyses large and complex datasets generated by genomics, pathology, radiology and electronic health records. AI may help identify actionable biomarkers, predict treatment response and resistance, support drug discovery, match patients to clinical trials and anticipate adverse drug reactions (ADRs). This review describes the principles of AI-driven precision oncology, major biomarkers, pharmacogenomics, mechanisms of selected targeted and immune therapies, drug-specific adverse effects, AI-assisted toxicity prediction, clinical workflow, advantages, limitations, ethical considerations and future directions. Selected therapies including osimertinib, trastuzumab, dabrafenib/trametinib, olaparib and pembrolizumab demonstrate how molecular findings can be translated into individualized treatment. The future of oncology is likely to involve multimodal AI combined with longitudinal molecular monitoring and multidisciplinary clinical decision-making.
